layer: Hypotheses: our reading of what happened in each case
rules: This file is ours, not the papers'. Facts about a case live in data/cases.json; if hypothesising turns up a factual error, fix the case record there.
Every entry rates all seven boring explanations before proposing a mechanism. A case beats the null only when none is Likely.
Hypotheses are ranked, each with a confidence, the specific variable driving the uncertainty, and an observation that would tell it apart from the next one.

null_explanation.natural_history: Natural history: spontaneous or episodic remission at this chronicity
null_explanation.regression: Regression to the mean: the patient presented at a peak
null_explanation.misdiagnosis: Misdiagnosis or secondary syndrome: the syndrome was driven by the condition being treated, or was something else
null_explanation.cointervention: Co-intervention: another treatment change, admission, adherence or circumstance at the same time
null_explanation.nonspecific: Non-specific suppression: sedation, sickness, apathy, cognitive or motor loss reduced all behaviour, not the syndrome itself
null_explanation.expectancy: Expectancy, placebo or attention: for functional disorders, suggestion may be the mechanism itself, so say so
null_explanation.reporting: Reporting artefact: selective reporting, single observer, no measure, overclaim

verdict.Beats the null: No boring explanation is Likely; at least one specific feature (reversal, timing, specificity) separates it from chance
verdict.Doesn't beat the null: At least one boring explanation is Likely
verdict.Undecided: The paper doesn't give enough to judge

natural_history.why: Five or six years of rituals stopping on the day of a stroke.

regression.why: No peak at presentation; the change was abrupt.

misdiagnosis.why: Onset around 68, no diagnosis, no scale, no treatment; five or six bottles of cold medicine a day looks as much like habitual use as compulsion.

cointervention.why: No new medicines and nothing else changed.

nonspecific.why: She couldn't recall breakfast, said she knew nothing, and had little speech or facial expression: genu infarcts cause amnesia and abulia, and someone who initiates less and forgets more drops rituals along with everything else.

reporting.why: Family report only; she still wore her gloves at day 10, against the 'abrupt' stop.

entries.verdict_note: The timing is striking, but the documented amnesia and loss of drive explain the change without anything OCD-specific. Drive and memory were never re-measured at 4 months, the one measurement that would have decided it.

hypotheses.claim: A strategic thalamocortical disconnection took away drive and memory, and the rituals went with other self-started behaviour.
hypotheses.chain: Genu infarct → cuts the anterior and inferior thalamic peduncles (thalamus to frontal cortex) → abulia and amnesia → fewer self-initiated acts, rituals included
hypotheses.for: Amnesia, reduced speech and facial expression documented; the recognised capsular genu syndrome.
hypotheses.against: Daily activities were said to be relatively preserved, and the rituals were still gone at 4 months, when abulia often eases.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Apathy and memory weren't re-measured at 4 months, so we don't know whether drive recovered while the rituals stayed away.
hypotheses.test: Rituals still absent after drive and memory recover points to the second hypothesis; rituals returning as apathy lifts confirms this one.

hypotheses.claim: The infarct interrupted the orbitofrontal-thalamic loop that sustains compulsions, a natural capsulotomy (the authors' reading).
hypotheses.chain: Genu lies beside the anterior limb targeted by capsulotomy → frontothalamic fibres cut → loop activity damped → compulsions stop
hypotheses.for: Close to the capsulotomy target; still gone at 4 months; the library's other OCD-ending lesions sit in the same loop (putamen, thalamus, frontal).
hypotheses.against: Genu, not anterior limb; no scale; the diagnosis is uncertain; the global deficits explain the change without it.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: The OCD diagnosis itself is uncertain (no criteria, no scale), so even a specific effect may not be an effect on OCD.
hypotheses.test: Lesion network mapping from the published CT figure: does it connect to the same network as the library's other OCD-ending lesions?

entries.questions: Was the daily cold-medicine intake compulsion or dependence? If dependence, this is partly a substance case.

natural_history.why: Three responses within a day of each start don't fit spontaneous fluctuation.

regression.why: Months of steady symptoms before; the change was abrupt and repeated.

misdiagnosis.why: Recurrent depression and anxiety diagnosed by her psychiatrist; no sign of bipolarity on history or screening.

cointervention.why: Antidepressants were switched a few weeks in, though after the first response and with only partial benefit.

nonspecific.why: Niraparib caused insomnia, not sedation; the change was a lift, not a damping.

expectancy.why: Each restart was known to her, and a cancer treatment invites hope; short-lived lifts fit expectancy too.

reporting.why: Recalled at a 10-month interview; no scores during the responses.

entries.verdict_note: Three exposures, three responses within about a day, each fading over 10 to 14 days. Rechallenge is the strongest feature a single case can have, and the built-in time limit is itself a clue. Expectancy is the main rival.

hypotheses.claim: PARP inhibition briefly damped neuroinflammatory signalling, lifting mood within hours until compensation set in.
hypotheses.chain: Niraparib → PARP1 blocked → less NF-κB activation and IL-1β release → monoamine and glutamate signalling recover → mood lifts; compensation within two weeks
hypotheses.for: PARP1 drives NF-κB and cytokines; minocycline, an antidepressant in trials, also inhibits PARP (the authors' point).
hypotheses.against: Under 12 hours is fast for an anti-inflammatory route; no inflammatory markers were measured.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No inflammatory markers before or during a response, so the route can't be checked in her.
hypotheses.test: CRP and IL-6 before and a day after a restart, alongside a mood rating; or the same quick response to another PARP inhibitor.

hypotheses.claim: PARP inhibition conserved NAD+ and shifted neuronal energy metabolism quickly, with tolerance over two weeks.
hypotheses.chain: Niraparib → PARP stops consuming NAD+ → NAD+ and sirtuin/mitochondrial activity rise → rapid change in neuronal energetics → mood lifts; homeostatic adjustment by two weeks
hypotheses.for: The speed and the tachyphylaxis suit an acute metabolic shift better than slow immune remodelling.
hypotheses.against: Entirely inferred from pharmacology; nothing in the case measured energetics; 100 mg worked as well as 300 mg.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No biomarker of any kind; this rests on what the drug does, not on anything observed in her.
hypotheses.test: Patient-reported mood in PARP-inhibitor trial data, by drug and by days since each dose start.

related.why: Minocycline, also a PARP inhibitor, improving bipolar depression

natural_history.why: Sixty-three years of near-daily hallucinations, gone within eight days.

regression.why: Not presenting at a peak; seen for weight loss.

misdiagnosis.why: Visual and command hallucinations from age 7, depression since the 1940s and repeated self-harm: possibly not schizophrenia alone, which changes what a diet could act on.

cointervention.why: Weight loss, more energy and closer clinic contact came with the diet; she also had sleep apnoea.

nonspecific.why: More energy, not less.

expectancy.why: An enthusiastic, closely followed new regimen.

reporting.why: Self-report only; no scale; ketosis never measured.

entries.verdict_note: Abrupt loss of lifelong hallucinations a week into a diet, held for a year, is hard to put down to chance. Which part of the diet did it is wide open, and the lapses without recurrence are the most interesting clue.

hypotheses.claim: Ketosis changed brain energy metabolism and excitability, the anticonvulsant mechanism, damping hallucinations.
hypotheses.chain: Under 20 g carbohydrate → hepatic ketones → β-hydroxybutyrate as neuronal fuel; GABA up, glutamate release down, mitochondrial efficiency up → perceptual network hyperexcitability damped
hypotheses.for: Eight days matches the onset of ketosis plus a few days; the library's ketogenic context records report similar gains in deliberate trials.
hypotheses.against: Ketosis was never confirmed, and lapses of several days back onto carbohydrate didn't bring the voices back.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No ketone measurement, so we don't know she was in ketosis at all.
hypotheses.test: Ketones during a lapse: voices staying away while out of ketosis would mean the effect isn't ketosis itself.

hypotheses.claim: Removing gluten removed an immune or exorphin trigger (the Dohan hypothesis, the authors' lead).
hypotheses.chain: Bread, pasta and potatoes gone → no gluten exposure → less gut-derived immune activation or opioid-like peptides → psychosis settles
hypotheses.for: Gluten-free diets help a subgroup in small trials (authors).
hypotheses.against: Anti-gliadin IgG negative; lapses onto bread and pasta didn't bring the voices back.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Serology was taken three months into the diet, when it would be negative anyway.
hypotheses.test: Coeliac serology before starting, or a blinded gluten challenge.

hypotheses.claim: Weight loss and better sleep apnoea improved sleep and arousal, and the hallucinations eased.
hypotheses.chain: Weight loss → less obstructive apnoea → better sleep and oxygenation → fewer hallucinations
hypotheses.for: She had obstructive sleep apnoea and morbid obesity; the library has a CPAP remission of a schizophrenia-like illness.
hypotheses.against: About 5 kg lost by day 26 is too little to change apnoea in 8 days.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Sleep and apnoea were never reassessed.
hypotheses.test: A sleep study or Epworth score before and after.

natural_history.why: An illness of about a year; some early psychoses remit after a poor start, though rarely off all medicines for eight years.

regression.why: Stable, severe symptoms through the trial isolation.

misdiagnosis.why: Psychosis began within about a year of the leukaemia: a leukaemia-related or paraneoplastic process cured by the transplant would make this a secondary psychosis.

cointervention.why: Methotrexate, ciclosporin and tacrolimus are immunomodulators; paradoxical improvement off antipsychotics can't be excluded (authors).

nonspecific.why: Back at full-time work.

reporting.why: PANSS and GAF documented; eight-year follow-up.

entries.verdict_note: Treatment-resistant psychosis gone within a month of the transplant, off all antipsychotics, and still gone eight years later. The two live rivals, an occult leukaemia-driven psychosis and the immunosuppressants given afterwards, would both still make this an immune story.

hypotheses.claim: Replacing the immune system removed an immune driver of the psychosis.
hypotheses.chain: Conditioning ablates host immune cells → donor haematopoiesis (and, over months, marrow-derived cells in the brain) → loss of autoreactive or pro-inflammatory clones → psychosis remits
hypotheses.for: Remission tracked engraftment and lasted eight years off antipsychotics; the mirror case, psychosis after a transplant from a donor with schizophrenia, is cited by the authors.
hypotheses.against: Microglial replacement takes longer than 30 days (the authors' own point); no immune markers or autoantibodies were tested.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No pre-transplant autoimmune work-up (neuronal antibodies, CSF), so antibody-mediated psychosis can't be told from a broader immune reset.
hypotheses.test: Stored pre-transplant serum or CSF tested for neuronal surface antibodies; similar remissions in other transplanted patients with psychosis.

hypotheses.claim: Post-transplant immunosuppression suppressed T-cell-driven inflammation, and the psychosis remitted under it.
hypotheses.chain: Methotrexate, ciclosporin, then tacrolimus → T-cell activation suppressed → less neuroinflammation → psychosis eases
hypotheses.for: Calcineurin inhibitors were started at day 0 and week 3, just before the improvement.
hypotheses.against: The remission lasted years, presumably after immunosuppression stopped.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: We aren't told when immunosuppression ended relative to the sustained remission.
hypotheses.test: Whether psychosis stayed away after tacrolimus was withdrawn.

hypotheses.claim: The psychosis was secondary to the leukaemia (paraneoplastic or CNS involvement), and treating the leukaemia ended it.
hypotheses.chain: Pre-clinical leukaemia → cytokines or CNS infiltration → psychosis → transplant cures the leukaemia → psychosis ends
hypotheses.for: Psychosis began within about a year of the leukaemia's presentation.
hypotheses.against: Normal MRI and EEG, no neurological signs; psychosis came up to a year before any leukaemia symptoms.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Blood counts at the onset of psychosis weren't reported.
hypotheses.test: A blood film or count from when the psychosis began.

natural_history.why: Decades of heavy drinking, stopped within two weeks.

regression.why: Came for depression treatment, not at a drinking crisis.

misdiagnosis.why: If the drinking was self-medication for depression, it ended because the depression did.

cointervention.why: Twice-weekly supervised clinic visits; a motivational session after the binge.

nonspecific.why: More active and working, not less.

expectancy.why: She sought ketamine after hearing another patient's story.

reporting.why: Abstinence self-reported, with no biomarkers or drinking scale.

entries.verdict_note: No boring explanation is Likely, but abstinence rests on self-report and the depression lifted alongside it. The case can't say whether esketamine acted on drinking or on the mood behind it.

hypotheses.claim: Esketamine acted on the drinking directly: NMDA blockade loosened drinking memories and reduced craving and impulsivity.
hypotheses.chain: Esketamine → NMDA blockade and a burst of plasticity → reconsolidation of drinking cues disrupted, less impulsivity → craving falls within two weeks
hypotheses.for: She reported less desire and impulsivity, not just better mood; ketamine has reduced drinking in small trials (recalled, not checked).
hypotheses.against: Her depression lifted at the same time; the binge on the lower dose fits a dose effect but also an ordinary lapse.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Mood and drinking changed together and were never measured separately over time.
hypotheses.test: Session-by-session craving ratings alongside PHQ-9: craving falling before mood would favour a direct effect.

hypotheses.claim: Drinking was self-medication for depression, and lifting the depression removed the reason to drink (the authors' reading).
hypotheses.chain: Esketamine → rapid antidepressant effect → less dysphoria, anger and anxiety → less drive to drink
hypotheses.for: Lifelong depression came first; anger and anxiety settled along with the drinking.
hypotheses.against: Earlier antidepressants failed, so there's no test of whether mood relief alone stops her drinking.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Same as above: no separate timeline for mood and drinking.
hypotheses.test: Whether drinking returns if the depression relapses while esketamine continues.

natural_history.why: Episodic depression and self-injury with long quiet stretches would look like this.

regression.why: Admitted at a crisis peak in a highly stressful setting; calm days later on a medical ward is what regression looks like.

misdiagnosis.why: Functional seizures (the authors considered them), dissociation (no memory of the behaviours) or trauma-related symptoms.

cointervention.why: A change of setting, intravenous levetiracetam and intensive care.

nonspecific.why: Postictal state and levetiracetam can flatten behaviour, though she was alert and engaged.

reporting.why: No score before the seizure, five days of observation, and no history from her about past episodes.

entries.verdict_note: Remission was judged a day after a seizure and a move out of custody, with nothing measured before and nothing after five days. She has had seizures for years, so if seizures lifted her mood it should have shown before.

hypotheses.claim: The crisis settled with the move from custody and a state hospital to a medical ward.
hypotheses.chain: Acute stress and confinement → self-injury and voices → transfer to a medical ward, intensive care, attention → crisis eases within days
hypotheses.for: Self-injury happened in custody and on admission; calm within days of a medical admission.
hypotheses.against: Voices and depression had reportedly persisted across settings for years.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No measure before the seizure, so we don't know how ill she was in the days before it.
hypotheses.test: Her symptoms on return to the state hospital, still off psychotropics.

hypotheses.claim: The generalised seizure acted like a single ECT treatment.
hypotheses.chain: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure → widespread network and neurotrophic changes, as in ECT → mood and psychosis lift
hypotheses.for: A generalised seizure came just before the remission.
hypotheses.against: One ECT treatment rarely produces remission, and she has had many seizures without one.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Her seizure history: if earlier seizures never helped her mood, a seizure effect is unlikely.
hypotheses.test: Mood records around her previous seizures.

natural_history.why: Alcohol use disorder does remit without treatment, often after a crisis.

regression.why: Not presenting at a drinking peak; seen for the head injury.

cointervention.why: Supervised withdrawal in intensive care; a frightening injury; gabapentin continued.

nonspecific.why: Anosmia and loss of taste removed wine's taste and smell; mild memory problems.

entries.verdict_note: Craving itself vanished, not just drinking, after a small lesion in a known addiction node, and it held through a year with one stress-linked lapse. The anosmia is the dull rival the authors didn't discuss.

hypotheses.claim: Disrupting the orbitofrontal node of the addiction network abolished craving (the authors' lesion-network reading).
hypotheses.chain: 1 cm left orbitofrontal contusion → disconnection of a hub that potentiates urges via projections to the dorsal striatum → craving and compulsive drinking stop
hypotheses.for: The lesion's connectivity converges on the published smoking-remission network (inverse, r = −0.59, permutation p = 0.04).
hypotheses.against: The contusion had resolved on CT by a month while abstinence continued; matching with the opposite sign needs the claim that any disruption works; one relapse.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: The connectivity match is opposite in sign to the reference map, so the result depends on accepting that disruption in either direction works.
hypotheses.test: Other orbitofrontal lesions in the literature: do they end addictions, and with which connectivity sign?

hypotheses.claim: Post-traumatic anosmia and loss of taste removed the sensory reward of wine.
hypotheses.chain: Frontal head injury → olfactory damage → wine no longer smells or tastes of anything → cue-driven craving falls
hypotheses.for: Persistent anosmia and ageusia at the clinic visit; much of wine's pull is smell and taste.
hypotheses.against: Craving isn't only sensory, and she relapsed under stress (smell then unknown).
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Whether smell and taste had recovered by the time of the relapse isn't reported.
hypotheses.test: Serial smell testing against craving: craving returning as smell returns would favour this.

hypotheses.claim: A near-fatal drunken fall and intensive care stay reorganised her motivation to drink.
hypotheses.chain: Frightening alcohol-related injury → a turning point → stops drinking
hypotheses.for: Drinkers often stop after a frightening alcohol-related injury.
hypotheses.against: She described losing the urge, not resisting it; earlier crises hadn't stopped her.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No account of how she understood the injury.
hypotheses.test: Craving measures that separate losing the urge from resisting it.

natural_history.why: Some schizophrenia settles over seven years, though rarely so completely.

misdiagnosis.why: A well-described paranoid psychosis with command hallucinations.

cointervention.why: Seven years under his mother's care with unknown medication; levetiracetam for seizures.

nonspecific.why: Severe frontal damage: apathy, aphasia with short answers, stimulus-boundedness. Less drive and less speech can mean less voiced psychosis.

reporting.why: Mother's report and interviews at 7 years; no psychosis scale.

entries.verdict_note: A modern leucotomy by gunshot: psychosis gone, but so is much of frontal function. With transcortical motor aphasia and apathy, whether the voices stopped or he stopped acting on and talking about them can't be told apart.

hypotheses.claim: Widespread frontal damage removed the drive and elaboration that kept the psychosis active, as leucotomy did.
hypotheses.chain: Bifrontal destruction → apathy, reduced initiative and emotional tone → delusions and voices no longer elaborated or acted on
hypotheses.for: FAB 4/18, apathy and stimulus-boundedness; the classic leucotomy picture.
hypotheses.against: He denies voices outright and is described as good-natured and sociable with people he knows.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Aphasia limits how much inner experience he can report, so absent voices can't be confirmed.
hypotheses.test: A structured psychosis interview adapted for aphasia, or observation for responding to voices.

hypotheses.claim: Specific disconnection of frontal-temporal circuits generating the hallucinations (left temporal damage too).
hypotheses.chain: Left frontal and temporal destruction → loss of the speech-production and auditory-cortex coupling thought to generate voices → voices stop
hypotheses.for: Voices were the core symptom; the left temporal lobe was damaged too.
hypotheses.against: The damage is so extensive that any specific claim is untestable in this case.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No timing: we don't know if the voices stopped at once or over years.
hypotheses.test: Lesion network mapping of the 7-year CT against the hallucination lesion network.

natural_history.why: Twenty years of refractory illness and five months of twice-daily episodes, stopping after session 2.

regression.why: Steady at the same severity for five months.

cointervention.why: Daily clinic contact for four weeks; antidepressants unchanged for three months.

nonspecific.why: She became more active and functional.

expectancy.why: Open-label daily treatment; nobody expected an eating effect, but the second course was explicitly to prevent relapse.

reporting.why: A self-kept daily log; no eating-disorder scale.

entries.verdict_note: An abrupt stop after two sessions, a return two months after the course ended, and a second stop after one session of a second course. In both courses the bingeing improved before the mood did, which argues against eating simply following mood.

hypotheses.claim: High-frequency dorsomedial prefrontal stimulation strengthened top-down control over the binge urge.
hypotheses.chain: 10 Hz rTMS at dorsomedial prefrontal cortex → more activity in a control node underactive in bulimia → urge-to-act coupling weakened → binges and purges stop; mood follows
hypotheses.for: Change after session 2 and after session 1 of the second course; she described less urgency and more choice; eating changed before mood.
hypotheses.against: No impulsivity measure; one patient; open label.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No standardised eating-disorder or impulsivity measure, so the mechanism rests on her description.
hypotheses.test: A sham-controlled course with stop-signal or delay-discounting tasks before and after.

hypotheses.claim: The antidepressant effect of rTMS lifted the mood that drove the bingeing.
hypotheses.chain: rTMS → antidepressant effect → less dysphoria → less bingeing
hypotheses.for: Depression and bingeing remitted in the same course and returned together.
hypotheses.against: Bingeing stopped before mood improved, in both courses (BDI-II was rated daily).
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Both measures are self-report, so the order rests on her ratings alone.
hypotheses.test: Daily mood and urge ratings through a repeat course.

natural_history.why: Agonist-driven impulse control disorder on an unchanged dose doesn't usually stop by itself.

regression.why: Started at a crisis: affairs and a US$30,000 spending debt.

misdiagnosis.why: A typical dopamine-agonist impulse control disorder.

cointervention.why: The marital and financial fallout may have motivated restraint.

nonspecific.why: GLP-1 agonists suppress appetite and may blunt drive in general.

expectancy.why: Semaglutide was for his kidneys; nobody expected this.

reporting.why: Self-report only; no impulse control scale.

entries.verdict_note: An effect that wears off the day before each weekly dose and returns when the drug runs out is a dose-response and a rechallenge in one patient, with the agonist that caused the disorder held constant.

hypotheses.claim: GLP-1 receptor activation damped the mesolimbic reward signalling that the dopamine agonist had sensitised.
hypotheses.chain: Semaglutide → GLP-1 receptors in ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens → less dopamine release to rewards → over-valuation of sexual and shopping rewards dampened
hypotheses.for: End-of-dose return and relapse on running out; semaglutide blunts alcohol-evoked dopamine release in rodents (authors).
hypotheses.against: Semaglutide's half-life is about a week, so a sharp wear-off the day before the next dose is more than drug levels alone predict.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Self-report only: no impulse control rating across the dosing cycle or the run-out.
hypotheses.test: A validated impulse control rating (such as QUIP-RS) across the injection cycle and a documented pause.

hypotheses.claim: General suppression of appetite and drive, not a specific effect on the impulse control disorder.
hypotheses.chain: Semaglutide → less hunger and less 'wanting' in general → fewer impulsive acts of every kind
hypotheses.for: GLP-1 agonists reduce food reward broadly.
hypotheses.against: He kept working and playing pickleball; motor drive and function stayed good.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Mood, apathy and other rewards weren't assessed.
hypotheses.test: An apathy scale alongside impulse control ratings.

natural_history.why: Heavy drinking fluctuates, and four years is not long.

regression.why: He came for weight loss, not at a drinking crisis.

misdiagnosis.why: Severe alcohol use disorder by DSM-5 count and AUDIT.

cointervention.why: Testosterone started the same week; weight-clinic contact; bipolar care elsewhere.

nonspecific.why: Appetite suppression and nausea cut intake of anything.

expectancy.why: He started semaglutide after hearing about others' success, though for weight.

entries.verdict_note: A 20-point AUDIT fall is real, but with testosterone started the same week, no timing and no biomarker, the case can only join the GLP-1 tally.

hypotheses.claim: GLP-1 receptor activation reduced the reward value of alcohol.
hypotheses.chain: Semaglutide → GLP-1 receptors in reward circuits → less dopamine response to alcohol → craving falls
hypotheses.for: He described the desire to drink disappearing; consistent with trials and the other GLP-1 cases here.
hypotheses.against: No record of when drinking fell relative to the dose steps.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No timeline of drinking against the titration schedule.

hypotheses.claim: Testosterone replacement improved mood and energy, and drinking fell with it.
hypotheses.chain: Testosterone for hypogonadism → better mood, energy and confidence → less drinking
hypotheses.for: Started the same week; hypogonadism can lower mood.
hypotheses.against: Testosterone isn't known to end heavy drinking.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No mood ratings, and the two drugs started together.
hypotheses.test: Drinking after either drug is stopped alone.

misdiagnosis.why: Two of three didn't have alcohol use disorder, so the 'syndrome' is mostly heavy drinking.

hypotheses.claim: GLP-1/GIP receptor activation reduced the reward value of alcohol.
hypotheses.chain: Tirzepatide → GLP-1 (and GIP) receptor signalling in reward circuits → less dopamine response to alcohol → drinking becomes boring
hypotheses.for: Case 1's craving fell within a month; case 2 found drinking boring; the other GLP-1 cases here.

hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Self-reported intake with no biomarker, in patients who all got new reasons to cut down.

hypotheses.claim: Gastrointestinal effects made drinking unpleasant.
hypotheses.chain: Tirzepatide → nausea, slowed gastric emptying, post-meal lethargy → alcohol less pleasant → less drinking
hypotheses.for: Case 3 had nausea for 3 days after each dose; case 1 had lethargy after meals.
hypotheses.against: The authors say drinking didn't fall because of lasting GI effects; case 3's nausea eased while intake stayed low.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Side effects weren't tracked against drinking.
hypotheses.test: Drinking across the weekly cycle: less on nausea days would favour this.

hypotheses.claim: Prefrontal iTBS strengthened top-down control over binge urges.
hypotheses.chain: Accelerated iTBS at left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex → more excitable inhibitory-control node → urge-to-binge coupling weakened → binges stop
hypotheses.for: Same timing in both; depression barely improved, so the effect looks specific; echoes Downar's dorsomedial case.

hypotheses.claim: Damage to frontal reward-regulation circuitry removed nicotine craving.
hypotheses.chain: Right frontal contusion and diffuse injury → disrupted frontostriatal reward circuitry → nicotine loses its pull → no craving or withdrawal

hypotheses.claim: Hospital-enforced abstinence during an acute illness broke the habit, and post-injury apathy kept it broken.

hypotheses.chain: Dulaglutide → delayed gastric emptying → fullness after a few beers → less drinking

hypotheses.claim: The haemorrhage disrupted a hyperactive left putaminal node in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop shared by OCD and psychosis.

hypotheses.against: A single lesion improving two disorders could also be non-specific, though none was found.

hypotheses.claim: Damage to the adjacent anterior limb of the internal capsule acted like a capsulotomy.
hypotheses.chain: Haematoma extends to the anterior limb → frontothalamic fibres cut → as in anterior capsulotomy, OCD remits

hypotheses.chain: Severe diffuse injury → reduced frontal-subcortical drive → obsessional drive gone

reporting.why: No follow-up length; the authors' group researches infection in bipolar disorder.

entries.verdict_note: A YMRS fall from 43 to 9 two weeks into anthelmintics, after months of failed drugs, is striking, but a delayed valproate response and the episode's natural end compete closely.

hypotheses.claim: A delayed response to valproate, or the episode running its natural course.
hypotheses.chain: Valproate from about three weeks before → full antimanic effect arriving; manic episodes end on their own over months
hypotheses.for: Valproate had just been added; the episode was already months old.
hypotheses.against: Months of adequate treatment had failed, and the change came abruptly at two weeks into anthelmintics.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No valproate levels and no dates for the episode's start.
hypotheses.test: Valproate levels and a YMRS series before the anthelmintics.

hypotheses.claim: Clearing the parasite removed a Th1-driven inflammatory push on mood circuits.
hypotheses.chain: Filarial infection → chronic Th1 inflammation (IFN-γ, TNF) → mood circuits destabilised → anthelmintics kill the parasite → inflammation settles → mania resolves
hypotheses.for: Active infection with hypereosinophilia; euthymia tracked parasite clearance (authors).
hypotheses.against: No inflammatory markers; filariasis is common and usually psychiatrically silent.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No cytokines or inflammatory markers before and after.
hypotheses.test: IL-6, TNF and eosinophils before and after, alongside YMRS.

hypotheses.claim: Albendazole or ivermectin acted directly: a Th2 shift or mitochondrial effects.
hypotheses.chain: Albendazole → Th2 cytokines (IL-5, IL-13) damp Th1 activity; ivermectin → mitochondrial effects → mood stabilised

hypotheses.against: Ivermectin barely enters the brain (authors); no supporting data in the case.
hypotheses.test: The same drugs in an uninfected patient with mania.

entries.verdict_note: The authors leave the cause open, rightly. Six months is about when resignation syndrome lifts with care, and everything else was changing too. What remains interesting is the abruptness within a week of the operation.

hypotheses.claim: Accumulated safety, support and hope reached a turning point, with the operation as a meaningful event for the family.
hypotheses.chain: Better housing and support over months → family hope renewed → child re-engages; the operation marks a turning point
hypotheses.for: Six months fits the usual course; the family's support had been renewed.
hypotheses.against: The change was abrupt, within a week of surgery.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Nothing documents the family's circumstances or hope at the time.
hypotheses.test: Recovery timing in similar children relative to asylum news and medical events.

hypotheses.claim: Relieving chronic pain and visceral distress (tethered cord, neurogenic bladder) removed a bodily driver of the withdrawal.
hypotheses.chain: Tethered cord → pain, urinary retention, constipation → distress feeding withdrawal → de-tethering relieves it → re-engagement
hypotheses.for: Within a week of de-tethering; bladder retention had worsened before surgery.

hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No pain or bladder measures around the operation.
hypotheses.test: Pain scores and bladder function before and after, against responsiveness.

entries.verdict_note: Y-BOCS fell from 25 to 3 with antiepileptics unchanged, and held at a year. Seizures only lessened, so the OCD fell further than the epilepsy did.

hypotheses.claim: Removing the right amygdala and hippocampus took out a limbic node feeding fear-driven obsessions.
hypotheses.chain: Right amygdala and hippocampus resected → loss of limbic input to the orbitofrontal-striatal loop → contamination fear and rituals fade
hypotheses.for: Y-BOCS 25 → 3 on unchanged antiepileptics; her fear aura and contamination fear both implicate the amygdala; similar lobectomy reports.
hypotheses.against: First reassessed at 6 months; seizures also fell.

hypotheses.claim: Fewer seizures and interictal discharges removed a seizure-driven part of the OCD.
hypotheses.chain: Epileptogenic focus removed → fewer discharges spreading to limbic and frontal circuits → OC symptoms fall

hypotheses.against: Seizures only lessened (ILAE class 2), yet the OCD nearly vanished.

hypotheses.test: Post-operative EEG and Y-BOCS together.

entries.verdict_note: Three men, the same rapid change once the dose was stable, restraints removed and the effect held for 5 to 16 months. What can't be told apart is whether behaviour improved in its own right or because the body stopped flailing.

hypotheses.claim: Less dystonia, ballism, pain and sleep loss removed the triggers and mechanics of the self-injury.
hypotheses.chain: Intrathecal baclofen → spinal GABA-B → spasticity, dystonia and ballism fall; sleep improves → fewer involuntary blows and less distress → self-injury stops
hypotheses.for: Dystonia scores fell by about three-quarters; sleep improved; ballism was abolished.
hypotheses.against: Lesch-Nyhan self-injury is compulsive and distressing, not just a by-product of movement.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Behaviour counts came from caregiver interviews, and motor symptoms improved at the same time.
hypotheses.test: Whether self-injury tracks dystonia scores across dose changes.

hypotheses.claim: GABA-B activation functionally opposed hypersensitive D1 signalling in the basal ganglia (the authors' reading).
hypotheses.chain: Baclofen → GABA-B receptors inhibit adenylyl cyclase, opposing D1 stimulation → less dopaminergic drive to self-injure
hypotheses.for: Fits the D1 supersensitivity model of Lesch-Nyhan self-injury.
hypotheses.against: Intrathecal baclofen acts mainly on the spinal cord; brain levels are low.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No way in the data to separate a central behavioural effect from the motor one.

hypotheses.chain: Seizure freedom → less fear, injury and disability; renewed control → arousal falls → PTSD, depression and functional seizures settle
hypotheses.for: All improved together within four weeks; functional seizures often stop after epilepsy surgery (authors).

hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No psychiatric scales before or after.

hypotheses.claim: Removing the right amygdala and hippocampus damped the fear circuitry behind the PTSD.
hypotheses.chain: Right mesial temporal resection → less amygdala-driven threat responding → PTSD symptoms fall

entries.verdict_note: The behaviour change is close to mechanical. The interesting residue is that weight and shape concern went too, which a missing stomach doesn't obviously explain.

hypotheses.claim: Losing the stomach removed both the capacity to binge and ghrelin-driven hunger and food reward.
hypotheses.chain: Total gastrectomy → no gastric reservoir and no gastric ghrelin → less hunger and hedonic drive, bingeing impossible → bulimic cycle broken
hypotheses.for: No stomach and no main ghrelin source; hedonic eating falls after bariatric surgery (authors).
hypotheses.against: Weight and shape concern also went, which mechanics alone don't explain.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No eating-disorder cognition measure before surgery, so the cognitive change is inferred.
hypotheses.test: Eating-disorder cognition scales and ghrelin levels in gastrectomy patients with earlier bulimia.

hypotheses.claim: A near-fatal illness and long nutritional rehabilitation reorganised her relationship with food and weight.
hypotheses.chain: Septic shock, emergency surgery, 35 days in hospital → months of structured feeding and follow-up → new eating pattern and attitude
hypotheses.for: A life-threatening crisis followed by intensive, structured care.
hypotheses.against: Many people with bulimia survive medical crises without remitting.
hypotheses.test: Her own account of what changed.

entries.verdict_note: A well-measured recovery, but the medication overhaul in hospital explains the parkinsonism and cognition, and plausibly the depression. The suicide attempt is the dramatic event, not necessarily the causal one.

hypotheses.claim: The medication overhaul: stopping perphenazine and anticholinergics cleared drug-induced parkinsonism and cognitive impairment, and escitalopram with mirtazapine treated the depression.
hypotheses.chain: Perphenazine/amitriptyline and earlier risperidone stopped → D2 blockade and anticholinergic load gone → parkinsonism and cognition recover; escitalopram + mirtazapine → depression remits
hypotheses.for: Parkinsonism and cognition recovered after the regimen changed; the second DaTSCAN was normal; the authors raise drug-induced parkinsonism.
hypotheses.against: Risperidone was low-dose and sulpiride long stopped; mirtazapine alone had failed for 13 months.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: The date perphenazine/amitriptyline stopped isn't given.
hypotheses.test: Dates of each drug change set against UPDRS and HAM-D.

hypotheses.claim: Surviving the attempt shifted her mood: relief after a brush with death.
hypotheses.chain: Life-threatening act → acute threat, then relief and changed meaning → mood lifts
hypotheses.for: Depression often lifts after a suicide attempt (authors).
hypotheses.against: It usually returns within three months; this held for two years.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: The medication changes overlap the attempt completely.
hypotheses.test: Depression trajectories after suicide attempts with no change in regimen.

hypotheses.claim: Burns and critical illness produced an inflammatory and stress-hormone surge that reset mood circuits.
hypotheses.chain: Major burns → cytokine and cortisol surge, then recovery → mood circuits reset
hypotheses.for: Severe physiological stress came just before remission.
hypotheses.against: No markers; nothing separates this from the drug changes.
hypotheses.test: Mood outcomes after major burns in people with prior depression.

entries.verdict_note: The pattern of stealing when methylphenidate was lowest, fixed by an evening drug, is suggestive, but nothing is counted or timed, and the authors admit night may simply be when he had the chance.

hypotheses.claim: Methylphenidate strengthened prefrontal inhibitory control through dopamine and noradrenaline, and guanfacine covered the trough hours.
hypotheses.chain: Methylphenidate → more dopamine and noradrenaline in prefrontal cortex → better impulse control → less stealing; wears off at night → guanfacine (α2A agonist) covers the trough
hypotheses.for: Stealing clustered at night and before the morning dose, when methylphenidate is lowest; evening guanfacine fixed it.

natural_history.why: Unchanged for a year through every treatment.

misdiagnosis.why: Well-characterised schizoaffective psychosis with normal work-up.

cointervention.why: A second ECT course of 21 sessions ended days before; antibiotics; smoking stopped.

nonspecific.why: More initiative and pleasure, not less.

entries.verdict_note: A year of total resistance, then improvement within days of an infection that quadrupled the clozapine level. The puzzle is that she improved after clozapine was stopped and restarted lower, so whatever happened outlasted the spike.

hypotheses.claim: A brief supratherapeutic clozapine exposure did what ordinary levels hadn't, and the gain persisted (the authors' reading).
hypotheses.chain: Inflammation (IL-6 down-regulating CYP1A2) plus stopping smoking → clozapine level about fourfold → days of very high receptor occupancy → lasting adaptation → response holds at ordinary levels
hypotheses.for: The level rose about fourfold; improvement followed within days; nothing else new was started.
hypotheses.against: She improved after clozapine was stopped and restarted lower (266 µg/L), and the later rise to 709 µg/L added nothing, which a simple dose effect wouldn't predict.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: No unbound clozapine level: inflammation raises protein binding, so the total level overstates the active exposure (authors).
hypotheses.test: Whether other clozapine non-responders respond to a deliberately raised level.

hypotheses.claim: The inflammatory response itself (CRP 193) had an antipsychotic effect, as in the intercurrent-infection cases.
hypotheses.chain: Severe pneumonia → cytokine surge and fever → transient immune effect on psychosis circuits → improvement as recovery begins
hypotheses.for: Severe infection just before; the library's intercurrent-fever cases (Zuschlag 2016, Wagner-Jauregg).
hypotheses.against: Improvement came after the infection was treated, as inflammation subsided.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: Inflammation and drug level rose together, so they can't be separated.
hypotheses.test: CRP and clozapine level tracked separately across infection-associated improvements.

hypotheses.claim: A delayed response to the second ECT course in combination with clozapine.
hypotheses.chain: Clozapine plus 21 ECT sessions → cumulative neuroplastic effect → response appearing just after the course ended
hypotheses.for: Clozapine with ECT is the standard rescue for clozapine resistance, and 21 sessions had just been given.
hypotheses.against: No change at all through ten weeks of combined treatment until the infection.
hypotheses.uncertainty_driver: ECT ended at the same moment as the level spike.
hypotheses.test: Similar cases where ECT continued through an infection.

entries.verdict_note: Remission the day after a seizure, after four weeks of non-response, on three scales. The catch is that rTMS responses often begin around session 11, so timing alone can't separate the two.

hypotheses.claim: The seizure acted like a single ECT treatment, setting off rapid neurotrophic and monoamine changes.
hypotheses.chain: Seizure → widespread neuronal discharge → BDNF and monoamine receptor changes, as with ECT → mood lifts within a day
hypotheses.for: Next-day remission after weeks of non-response; ECT and magnetic seizure therapy work through seizures.
hypotheses.against: A brief focal or absence-type seizure, not a generalised one; single ECT treatments rarely bring remission.

hypotheses.claim: A delayed, cumulative rTMS response that happened to land the day after the seizure.
hypotheses.chain: Eleven high-frequency rTMS sessions → cumulative cortical plasticity → response emerging around session 11–12
hypotheses.for: About 11 sessions is when rTMS responses often begin.
